utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we have the appearances for today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier appearing for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in the proceedings. The Defence of Mr. Perisic is today represented in the courtroom by Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning, sir. Good morning. Just again to warn you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 709 displayed on the monitor. I'm interested in B/C/S page 25 and the English, page 23. Your Honour, I think it should be page 33 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct. Mr. Starcevic, what this is is a document you have seen before. This is a text from the stenographic record of the 14th Session of the SDC held on the 11 October 1993. I would like to direct your attention to the first paragraph in your document, and in the English version, the text that is found in the middle of the page, under Mr. Perisic's name, the second paragraph, starting with: "Another thing is of the essence here ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this text, I just want to refresh your recollection. Can you see it, Mr. Starcevic, the text?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found that piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's the top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And this text reads: "Another thing is of the essence here. They are asking for specific individuals. If those men refuse to go there, then we need to view them as deserters who don't want to defend their homes."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back into public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please wait.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have P875 displayed on the monitor. Could we first look at the -- what this document is, and could we go to the last page, as well, and see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is -- this is a document that is signed by the commander of the Main Staff of the SVK, Major-General Milan Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could return again to the first page of each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, this is a document dated the 14th of May. It is from the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina, and it's addressed to the Yugoslav Army General Staff. And it says: "In order to replenish the Republic of Serb Krajina aviation units, we require the following officers." And it has a long list of names and ranks of particular individuals. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain in what sense you expect that. But if I may say so, it is rather unusual to ask for specific individuals for replenishment or reinforcements of some units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, is there any legal basis for an army of a different country - in this case, the SVK - to request specific officers from the Yugoslav Army for replenishment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Then if we could turn to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 741. Could we first go to the last page of the document to see who the author of this document was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, this -- as you can see from the monitor, this is a document that was signed by General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could return now to the first part of the document, first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm interested -- first of all, this is a decision dated the 24th of March, 1994, and it's a decision on determining the task --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 24th or 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 22nd; I apologise. The 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it's a decision on determining the tasks where service is performed under difficult, special circumstances. Mr. Starcevic, have you seen this document before coming into court today?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first, let's focus on paragraph 1, if we could. Paragraph 1 defines to whom this -- this decision applies, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could now look at the second paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What does this paragraph define, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph defines the territory which is considered territory where duties are performed under difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could take a look at these various elements in here, I would like to focus on, particularly, item number 5. Could you tell me, first of all -- actually -- before we go to item number 5, are you familiar with these kinds of documents? Have you seen these kinds of documents before, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was always an order, "naredba," which defined the type of service that is considered service under difficult conditions, and I think this is one such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your understanding -- based on your past experiences, what is your understanding of the meaning of the term "service under difficult circumstances?" What kind of circumstances are mentioned or required to fill within that definition?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these circumstances can vary significantly, but they would mean that men would have to undergo additional efforts in order to perform their tasks. There could be all sorts of reasons, whether they be natural conditions or other conditions that are not normal conditions that are normal for most people in the Army of Yugoslavia. So these would be conditions either caused by man or some other conditions that simply require extra effort on the part of the troops, or it could entail an increased level of danger or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So they would be -- would it be fair to say they would be abnormal circumstances outside the normal realm of service in the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to characterise, Your Honour, generalise in a very short way to capture what the witness has said. If it is leading, I will withdraw the question if it's objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, what do you say? What's your submission? Is it or is it leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is leading, Your Honour, but I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, so then let me direct your attention to item number 4, subpart 4 of this document, and subpart 4 in this document identifies the authorised officer from Article 156 issues the decision on entitlement to this compensation for any person who meets the requirements for compensation from this decision. Can you tell us what the term "the authorised officer" means in the context of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An authorised officer is an officer who is authorised under Article 156 of the law, and as far as can I recall, if I'm not mistaken, this would be the chief of the General Staff or another officer -- no, no. No, this would be the officer commanding the unit where this service is performed, provided that he was at least at the level of battalion commander or higher. In other words, this should be an officer of a unit of at least a rank of battalion or higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And your answer says it would be an officer commanding the unit where this service is performed. Can you -- do you know on what territory the members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres were in service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The duty post for members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres was Belgrade, as we have seen from a previous document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. The seat of the Personnel Centres was at the -- or the headquarters was at the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any difficult or special conditions in Belgrade that would warrant this -- that would fall within the purview of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really wouldn't know that. These are operational issues, and that was not my field. As I said, I didn't even know that these centres existed at the time, so it is not really possible that I should know what territory they covered and what the conditions there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we now go to Prosecution Exhibit 1810.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, have you seen this document before coming into court?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is a document dated December the 5th, 1994, and it is issued by Military Post 3001, and it is a decision to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this December the 5th or the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm back in the American mode, Your Honour. I'm sorry. It is the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe we must outlaw the American mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I won't comment on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, what is this decision? Can you -- can you tell the Court what this decision is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the decisions that are required to be issued according to the order so that individuals would be entitled to hardship allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what is the authority? What's the basis of issuing this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- in essence, there are two legal bases for this decision. One of them is already the already-mentioned Article 156 of the law, authorising an officer to issue a decision on hardship allowance and special condition service; and the other foundation or basis is the already-mentioned order by the chief of the General Staff, which defines that entitlement in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention, Mr. Starcevic, to subpart (b) of this document. Now, this decision applies to General Ratko Mladic. In subpart (b) -- can you comment on subpart (b)?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is my impression that subpart (b) is not really a decision of any sort because no decision is made to increase compensation, and in my view, this is just a form that was used, but in this particular case the decision wasn't really made because we don't see the figure there indicating what the increase of compensation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. But there's a reference, is there not, to a decision of the commander of the -- of Military Post 3001, and there's an identification number, 21/32-21, dated the 3rd of February, 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do see that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I don't know what that decision is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, bearing in mind the earlier answer that the witness gave, that there are no figures there indicating what the amounts were, I think this is calling for the witness to speculate because he has already said in his earlier answer that he can't see that there was any decision because there is no figure put in there, so with this additional question, he is being called to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't ask him to speculate. I asked him if in fact there was this reference in subpart (b).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean you didn't see the reference, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The objection as I understood it was he is called to speculate. I didn't ask him to speculate. My question to him was, there is an reference to a decision, and I cited the decision and that reference number. That's all I did, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could turn to the next document, which is Prosecution Exhibit 399.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can see, first of all, that this is a document that is dated the 3rd of February, 1994, and it bears the same reference number that was seen on the previous document, 21/32-21, and it is a decision on the compensation for military service in difficult (special) circumstances, and it was issued by the General Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of the document to see who issued this document. That is not the last -- I'm sorry, it should be the second-to-last page on the English because those just show who the copies were sent to. If we go to the previous page, page 2. We see at the bottom of the page, there is an indication of who issued this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see a signature at the bottom of that page, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And whose signature or whose name is that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we go back to the first part of this -- the first page of this document. Now, you have seen this document before, Mr. Starcevic, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, this is a document whereby the Main Staff of the VRS, the Republika Srpska army, indicates what the compensation -- the level of compensation will be for difficult conditions, for military service under difficult conditions, and, of course, that would also depend on the unit where such service is performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this document define to whom this decision applies?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is that reference found in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this decision issued by General Mladic applies special compensation, and I will read paragraph 1: "... to all professional soldiers and NCOs, civilians in the army, officers and NCOs and contract soldiers serving in the Yugoslav Army deployed in the army of the Republika Srpska are entitled to compensation for carrying out military service in difficult conditions ..." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have seen from the previous document that General Mladic was awarded compensation for serving under difficult circumstances. Can you -- do you have any observations on -- on that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, it is the way you put it. Any kind of compensation to members of the Army of Yugoslavia is issued when they are deployed in the army of Republika Srpska. This is according to paragraph 1 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this question, Mr. Starcevic. This is a reference -- I'm sorry, the previous document had a reference to the document that's now before you, a document issued by the VRS. The previous document was issued by a unit of the VJ by the 30th Personnel Centre. Is there a reason, in your view, or a basis in your view, why a decision which was issued by the 30th Personnel Centre would have a reference to a decision issued by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reason that I can see is that the decision does not determine specific amounts of the compensation but only the general right to compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. The previous document that we looked at where there was no entry filled in subpart (b) said that the increase of compensation which was mentioned in above and the decision -- and so -- I'm sorry. Let me go back again. I'm sorry. It said --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we go back to Prosecution Exhibit 1810; put that on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if this is a VJ form, why is there reference in subpart (b) to a decision of the commander of Military Post 3001, the document that was issued by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was a -- a model of the Army of Yugoslavia, but actually, it's a form that was applied in a specific military post, and then it was prepared for all cases in the future. In this specific case, in the view of the person who made the decision, there are no elements to recognise this increase for Mr. Mladic. So I assume that out of technical or bureaucratic reasons they prepared forms in advance, and then specific parts of the forms would be filled in as per need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can't resist asking you, Mr. Harmon, about your question at page 13, lines 9 to 11. Your reference to VRS there, where do you pick it up from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I picked it up in the previous document because there's a reference, 21/32-21, with a date. That is Prosecution Exhibit 399. A caption of that document is General Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, so that's why I carried -- that's where I make the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you have made us look at this document that is on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question to the witness is, having put this document: "Mr. Starcevic, if this is a VJ form ..." and this is what you contend is a VJ form, "... why is there reference in subparagraph (b) ..." here, "... to a decision of the commander of Military Post 3001, the document that was issued by the VRS?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, where is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The document that was issued by the VRS is 21/32-21, which is dated the 3rd of February, 1994, and it is the same document that I showed earlier, P399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But there are two documents that have this reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What precedes the one -- which one precedes the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The VRS document is -- P399 is dated the 3rd of February, 1994, and the VJ document that we have on the screen, P1810, is dated 12th of May, 1994. So General Mladic's order or decision precedes the document that is now before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And haven't we seen this morning a document, I don't know whether it was P741, which is a general decision of the VJ which tells you where the circumstances under which VJ soldiers operating under different circumstances would be generally entitled to compensation, and the very last category mentioned is 30th and 40th Personnel Centres?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And I asked the witness if he knew where and on which territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, but what I'm saying, that document, what is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document is the 22nd of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Still came after the VRS document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then there is something I don't understand. Let me not ask the question. Maybe the evidence will explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me try to approach this a different way, Mr. Starcevic. The word "decision" has a very precise meaning in a military context, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judge what the term "decision" means in the military context?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the remark that not only in the military context but also in the legal system, in our country, in Yugoslavia, a decision is usually an administrative document that decides on the right or duty of a specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And is it unusual or -- I'm sorry. Have you ever seen in a decision issued by the VJ a decision that grants rights, which decision is from a different army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand, but I think that this is not possible in the legal sense either. It's not possible in the legal sense because authority is determined under two criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions on this particular set of documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question remains unanswered. Anyway, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have the next exhibit, which is Prosecution Exhibit 2625.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it should be 65 ter 2625 [Microphone not activated]. I apologise. 65 ter 2625.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this document is a decision dated the 6th -- 2nd of June, 1994, and is issued by Military Post 7111. My first question is: Do you know where Military Post 7111 is? Are you familiar with that reference?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really, but you can see from the decision that it's in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, and where is Han Pijesak? In which country is Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This decision relates to Captain Dragan Obrenovic, who is serving in Military Post 7469 in Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Focus on subpart (b) of this document. Is this decision to grant Captain First Class Dragan Obrenovic additional compensation based on the previous document we looked at, which was the decision of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any comments in respect of this document, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that everything that we said before applies to this document as well. I don't know specifically what you're thinking of, but from this decision, it is evident that Mr. Obrenovic met the required conditions in the order of General Mladic in order to receive an increase of the hardship allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we looked at General Mladic's previous order and to whom it applied. It applied to soldiers serving in the Yugoslav Army deployed in the army of the Republika Srpska. Can you make any comments in respect of the status of Captain Obrenovic, based on the two documents that we have looked at?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the condition was for the soldier to be a member of the army of Yugoslavia, then, on the basis of that, it transpires that Mr. Obrenovic is a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could now go into private session, please -- actually, first of all, I would like to take look at Prosecution Exhibit 363, is the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going show you a series of three documents, Mr. Starcevic, and then I'm going to ask you some questions about them because there is a similarity. Could we first go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Harmon is going to tender this document for admission or he might intend to do it later? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll do it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will tender the document now for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2303.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a series of documents, Mr. Starcevic. This first document is a document that is issued by Military Post 4795, and it's a certificate certifying that a particular individual was wounded while serving compulsory service at 4795 Belgrade military post. First of all, do you know what post designation that is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have personal knowledge, but I know that it's a military post that is located in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to direct your attention to the second paragraph. It indicates that this individual was wounded on the 2nd of January, 1994, while carrying out combat activities, i.e., securing the SRJ, Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, state border. This is the first of --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Federal republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I want to now discuss with you legal provisions that would apply to General Perisic in his capacity as chief of the General Staff that relate to his capacities, his ability to discipline, punish, or sanction individuals who he has knowledge of committed crimes or breaches of discipline. So, first of all, I'd like to focus on military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could return to Prosecution Exhibit 197. I'd like to turn to, first of all -- could we turn to chapter 8 of this document, and particularly Article 159, and that's found at page 14 of the B/C/S. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Specifically, if we can turn to page 14 of the B/C/S and page 39 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Starcevic, I want to focus, as I say, on Article 159. Can you -- and 159 from the text makes a distinction between a disciplinary infraction which is a minor violation of discipline -- and a disciplinary offense, which is a serious violation of military discipline. Can you enlighten us as to what constitutes a minor violation and a serious violation within the meaning of Article 159?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from Article 159, a minor violation of military discipline is defined in general terms, and this includes any type of violation whose consequences are not too serious, or extremely serious, in terms of military service. Serious violation of military discipline may be of different types; for instance, absent -- absence without leave from the place where one is serving, indecent behaviour, or similar. On the other hand, a serious violation of military discipline is such a violation that may lead to significant consequences in terms of the situation within units. In addition to these -- to these provisions that make a distinction in general terms between a disciplinary infraction and a disciplinary offence, a serious violation of military discipline, there are also -- there's also an additional regulation or, rather, a book of rules on military discipline which would be of greater assistance in defining what a military infraction or offence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to -- you have it on the screen before you, Article 160, and if we could go to the next page in the English. I direct your attention, Mr. Starcevic, to the first -- the top paragraph. Is this the definition of military -- a violation of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is a definition of one of the possible violations of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to -- if we look at this particular provision, this article, it lists 11 categories of -- 11 actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to subpart (10) of Article 160, which is: "An action in service which is contrary to military order or which represents a violation of existing regulations." What -- in this instance, can you just generalise for us what types of regulations there are that might fall under the purview of this provision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these would primarily be military regulations that regulate the activity of the army and military units and institutions as well as the responsibilities and duties of individuals. However, it would also encompass violations of some general regulations, not necessarily military regulations, but also civil regulations that are binding for any citizen of a country. And if a member of the army would commit a breach of such a regulation, that would at the same time constitute a breach of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter -- 65 ter 1995 on the screen. That doesn't ... perhaps the next page. That doesn't appear to be what I'm looking for. I'm looking for the -- could we go to the next page in B/C/S perhaps. Is there a way to put that in the right order? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, what you see here -- can you tell us what you see on your screen? In the English, it appears to the Regulations on the Application of International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the exact translation from the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with these regulations, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how are you familiar with these regulations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in their drafting. As I said, among other things, I was also involved in matters relating to international law within the legal administration, and these are regulations that fall within the ambit of international humanitarian law. So I actually worked on drafting these regulations as a member of a larger team that prepared these regulations as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page we see before us is the date 1988. These regulations apply -- or were promulgated in 1988, obviously. They apply to the JNA. My question is: Did they also apply to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These regulations are still in force now within the army of Serbia because no new regulations have replaced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, we left off, we were just -- I had just introduced this subject of these regulations on the Application of the International Laws of War in the Armed Forces within the SFRY. I'd now like to direct your attention to three articles in these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go first to Article 20, which is found on B/C/S, page 16, and English, page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you -- actually, I see that Article 20 is only partially reproduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have to go to the next page, as well, Your Honours, on this. So I would perhaps let Your Honours read Article 20, the first part of it that appears, and let you read the complete article before I ask some questions, so ... When Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in the English or scroll down --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- whatever the case is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Starcevic, can you just explain to us the -- Article 20 of these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply said, this article defines the accountability of any individual who commits a crime according to the international law of war under these regulations. So anyone who commits such a crime or orders the commission of such a crime is held -- is to be held accountable, is responsible, and this is personal responsibility. And it also defines that the primary responsibility for determining the accountability is -- are the national laws or the -- national courts of law, or the courts of a foreign state, if that person should fall into their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I see from the last paragraph in Article 20 that it applies to people not only who commit crimes but people who organise, incite, or assist in the commission of crimes. Is that correct? Perhaps it is not reproduced in your Article 20. If we go to --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is not reproduced -- not visible in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. So not only those who commit a crime but also accomplices, and persons who aid and abet, they also are accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we take a look at the next article, Article 21, could you focus your attention on that article, please, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In essence --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before I ask you the question, Mr. Starcevic, I want to give the Judges the opportunity to read that particular article, and then I'll ask you to explain the purpose and meaning of Article 21, or Regulation 21. Could you now then, Mr. Starcevic, explain the purpose and meaning in Regulation 21?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, this defines command responsibility; in other words, the responsibility of officers for acts committed by their subordinates and which constitute violations of humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you discuss with us for a moment the provision that is found in the second full sentence of the regulation, starting with: "The officer shall also be held personally liable ..."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In these instances, an officer who fails to take measures to determine the liability or responsibility of an individual, that officer would be responsible as an accomplice or incite -- as the person inciting or instigating a crime because that is considered to contribute to a renewed or another criminal act being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now turn to the third regulation, Regulation 36. It's found on B/C/S, page 21; in the English, on page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, in the English version we find that 36 is only partially reproduced, and we have to go to the next page, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, then, the continuation of the regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, could you discuss the purpose and intent of this particular regulation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 36, in fact, makes it obligatory on military officers to -- once they have learned that a criminal act has been committed, to collect and keep certain evidence and initiate proceedings either before a military prosecutor directly; in other words, by forwarding the evidence to the military prosecutor or via their superior officer. But in any case, they are duty-bound to prevent further violations of the international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is the consequence, Mr. Starcevic, if a Yugoslav Army officer learns of violations of the laws of war and does not implement any of these regulations we have been discussing, including Article 36, which orders -- which requires the -- an investigation and evidence to be collected?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences are listed in the earlier article that we've seen, Article 21, whereby an officer who fails to do so is responsible as an accomplice or an instigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me turn back to Prosecution Exhibit 197. I would like to go to Article 161 again. We've seen that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we looked at this -- I'm sorry, 160 is what I'm interested in, not 161. If we could just go up a little higher in the English. Thank you. We looked at this earlier, Mr. Starcevic, and particularly we focussed on subpart (10). Would a violation of the regulations that we just discussed and we just looked at constitute a violation of military discipline within the ambit of Article 160 of the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some less serious cases, yes, and that would constitute a violation of military discipline, or, rather, it could be put under the umbrella of Article 10 or subpart (10).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at another article in P197.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to B/C/S, page 6; in the English, page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could look, Mr. Starcevic, at Article 64. Could you just discuss with us the purpose and intent and meaning of Article 64 found under the chapeau "removal from duty."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this article has a twofold purpose: On the one hand, to protect the office or the service from persons who are responsible or who are in fact prevented from performing their duty; and, at the same time, to allow some other individual to perform that duty or that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, in the text of this article, if we look at the paragraph that starts with: "A professional soldier may be removed from duty if he was caught ..." If we look at that text, at the end of that text it -- paragraph, it says --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "... and the criminal act or disciplinary offence is of such a nature that it would be damaging to the interests of service that such an individual should remain on duty." Now, would a breach of the regulations that we just looked at a minute ago fall within the ambit of Article 64? In other words, would they be damaging to the interests of the service, and would they -- would they -- could they result in the invocation of Article 64?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could, but in the final analysis, this is left to the discretionary right of the person who is authorised to decide on removal of service. But generally speaking, it can be -- the reason for such an assessment could be the damage done to the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was General Perisic authorised to decide on the removal of professional officers from the service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be -- strike that. If a war crime was known to a superior officer, chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, would that person have the discretion to remove the offending officer from service in the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we -- I would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to remove such an individual from service. However, whether that person would also be discharged from the army is something that would be decided in a different type of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let's make that distinction very clear. Could you expand on that, what you mean by that, remove from the service versus discharge from the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An individual is removed from duty temporarily until proceedings that were instigated because the person was removed from duty are completed, and only once such proceedings are completed can there also be discussion on whether that individual would also be discharged from service from the army. For instance, if a criminal proceeding -- if criminal proceedings have been instigated against someone for a criminal act, that person may and in some instances should be removed from duty. However, they would still remain as members of the army. Only once a final decision or a final judgement has been handed down in those criminal proceedings would it be determined or could it be determined whether that person would remain in the army or would be discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I move to introduce, then, the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number. That is it P197 -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's the regulations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just tell us exactly what is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just briefly, it we could turn to Article 161. That's found at page 14 of the B/C/S and page 40 of the English. I don't want to dwell too much on this article, but I just want to make sure it's clear what this is. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can I just get clarification on one little point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You -- sir, you have told us that, you know, Momcilo Perisic would be authorised to remove an officer from duty and then the proceedings would carry on, and whether or not a determination was to be made on his dismissal -- discharge from the army would be made after the proceedings. Who would make the determination whether he should be discharged from the army? Who would be authorised to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some cases, those authorities -- that authorisation is also within the purview of General Perisic. In some instances it would be with other officers, but that would primarily depend on the rank and position of the individual involved. In other words, in some instances, General Perisic was the authorised individual. He was authorised for individuals up to the rank of colonel. If I recall, there were such regulations defining this. For instance, if someone was to -- if -- if ranks from the level of general were concerned, I think that the authority was with the president of the republic, but for individuals under that level and under the level of colonel, there would be other officers who would be responsible other than General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who are the other officers other than General Perisic who would be authorised to do so? I'm not asking for a name. I'm asking for a position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Well, it is difficult to answer that question in this particular -- at this particular time without looking at this other regulation. But I would like to remind you that according to Article 152 of the army, the chief of the General Staff or the officer -- the commanding officer of a unit that he determines, and I assume that in this particular case there was an order adopted at the General Staff regulating the responsibilities of those other officers. For instance, in my earlier experience, this could have been a commander of a corps or perhaps commanding officers at the level of brigade or regiment. They would be responsible for some lower-level officers and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they could discharge an officer from the army once there is proof -- once the process has gone through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in some cases, yes. Sometimes they would be duty-bound to do so if an officer is sentenced to a prison term of -- I think the cut-off line was six months or a year, but in our earlier laws, it was two years. I think under the new law this cut-off line is somewhat lower. So if someone was sentenced to that certain prison term, then the officer, the superior officer was duty-bound to also issue a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A declaratory decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Starcevic, I wanted to direct your attention very, very briefly to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I wanted to direct your attention very briefly to Article 161. Can you -- first of all, let me give the Judges an opportunity to read 161, and then I'd just like you to distinguish that from the previous article. Mr. Starcevic, what is the intention and purpose of Article 161, and to whom does it apply?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it applies to all professional officers as well. What is its purpose? Article 160 regulates violations of military order, military regulations, military duty; that is to say, all proceedings are related -- all acts are related to the army. However, according to Article 161, a violation of military discipline can also be in the form of violation of some other values which are not necessarily linked to the protected military values, which means that a commission of a crime can come under this heading. And other thing that was quite typical for our regulations was any expression of racial, ethnic, or religious intolerance, violation of public morals, and so on. It doesn't need to be necessarily linked to the army. It could be some kind of a social event that can lead to this type of violation, which would be outside of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I was going to -- I wanted to clarify that point where it says in the text itself of the first paragraph: "Every action of a service member outside of service ..." Can you define that "outside of service" phrase?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Private conduct, private conduct of a person as a private individual. That is to say not as a service member, military member, but an ordinary citizen who lives and exists within a normal social framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly, as well, if we could take a look at Article 162. And again, in the English it is only partially reproduced there, so we would have to go to the next page. First of all, if I could let the Judges have an opportunity to read Article 162 on this page and the next page, and then we'll just ask you just very briefly to explain this. Briefly, Mr. Starcevic, what does this article do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article defines all persons that can be held responsible for disciplinary violation. It also specifies time or a particular point in time from which their disciplinary responsibility arises and, also, in some cases, until the point in time where it terminates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we can now focus on the next two articles. We'll start with Article 163, and it doesn't appear in the B/C/S on the text. I want to look at both 163 and 164 together. Mr. Starcevic, I think you've earlier distinguished between an disciplinary infraction and a disciplinary offence. Obviously, 163 by virtue of the text describes the consequences that can result from the commission of a disciplinary infraction. I want to focus your attention a little bit more on Article 164, which deals with the consequences that can result from conviction, if you will, of a disciplinary offence. Would I'd like to do first of all, Mr. Starcevic, is to direct your attention to subpart (5) of this Article 164; that is, the loss of the right to serve as a professional soldier. Who makes that determination?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All disciplinary violations are dealt with by military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Does anybody else have the authority to address that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except in appeals proceedings when this is dealt with by regular courts. At that time, we had a military court, supreme military court, and nowadays we have the supreme administrative court; that is, the court of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at subpart (6), which is the loss of rank, and I would be interested if you can explain that to us in conjunction with the last sentence in Article 164.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This means that there is a difference between the loss of rank and the loss of the right to serve. When somebody loses the right to right to serve, he maintains the rank that he had at the time of his discharge. However, if somebody is punished with the loss of rank, then the loss of service results from that. It is a legal consequence of the loss of rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Very briefly, if we could turn to just a description of the statute of limitations that relate to disciplinary offences. That's found in Article 166.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought you were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Article 166, then. Let me just direct your attention to some passages in this. First of all, this clearly defines the statute of limitations in respect of disciplinary offences and disciplinary infractions; correct? You have to answer audibly.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in part, this -- in the third paragraph, it says: "Starting and conducting proceedings for a disciplinary offence which is also a criminal act has a statute of limitations for the same period as for the prosecution of the criminal act." So -- can you explain that passage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A statute of limitations for crimes is regulated by another law, the Law on Criminal Proceedings. Since in disciplinary proceedings a crime comes up as a condition for instituting disciplinary proceedings, it's a condition to institute them, then it's it quite a logical solution. It cannot run out before the basic act, which was the pre-condition for a disciplinary proceedings runs out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- so in domestic law, there are statues of limitations for criminal acts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said the Law on Criminal Proceedings, but I was wrong. It should have been the Criminal Code. Yes, such a law exists, and once again, it is a pre-condition for launching disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, up to 1995, was it an offence in the Criminal Code to commit a violation of -- a war crime or a violation -- a genocide? Was that embedded in the domestic code as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It was in the old Criminal Code of the then SFRY. In that code, there was an entire chapter which was devoted to crimes against international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what the statues of limitations was for violations of international humanitarian law in the domestic Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes against international humanitarian law, that is to say, war crimes and crimes against humanity, the crime of genocide, they do not have a statute of limitations. The statute of limitations never runs out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So do I understand that for purposes of Article 166, commencement and the conduct of criminal proceedings for a disciplinary offence for the criminal act of genocide or violation of international humanitarian law would be limitless? It never runs out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interject. Sir, you answered at page 40 lines -- starting from line 19 to line 21 you said: "Yes, certainly. It was in the old Criminal Code of the then SFRY. In that code, there was an entire chapter which was devoted to crimes against international law." My question is, what is the position with respect to that question in the constitution of the FRY? Yes, in the Criminal Code of the FRY, not SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's the same situation. The statute of limitations doesn't run out when it comes to violations of international humanitarian law. It is also an international obligation, both of the -- both of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who is a signatory to the convention stating that the statute of limitations doesn't run out when it comes to genocide. It also means the application of that convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That answer did not relate to limitation. It related to something else. Let me tell what you the question was. The question had been: "Now, Mr. Starcevic, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia up to 1995, was it an offence in the Criminal Code to commit a violation of -- a war crime or a violation -- a genocide, was that embedded in the domestic code as well?" And then your answer was: "Yes, but it was in the old code." My question is, is a violation of international humanitarian law currently embedded in the domestic law, as well, in the Criminal Code of the domestic law of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if we can turn to Article 177 of this Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's found at page 15 of the B/C/S and page 45 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you distinguish for us the difference between the two types of courts that are described in Article 177?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first-instance military disciplinary courts are those courts which are established within the headquarters of some units, commands of some units. Higher military disciplinary court is a disciplinary court that deals with appeals from the decisions handed down by the first-instance military disciplinary courts. It should be noted that in both cases, the judges are not lawyers in both of these courts. Those are mostly officers of operative military units -- oh, I could call them general military officers; whereas secretaries of those courts, or clerks of those courts, are lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can we now turn your attention to Article 180. Could you explain to us, Mr. Starcevic, the meaning and intent of Article 180.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose here was to regulate the basic elements of the proceedings when it comes to disciplinary violations. This establishes who is responsible for initiating an investigation of a disciplinary breach and also decide whether this was a disciplinary infraction or a disciplinary violation. And then further on, this person has to forward the case to the person who is responsible to place the perpetrator formally under the jurisdiction of a military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, would General Perisic fall within the purview of Article 180?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In exceptional circumstances, yes, but before him, his subordinates who are in charge of units or institutions where perpetrator works, they would be responsible before him. General Perisic would be responsible if, for example, in General Staff there were officers who were directly subordinate to him without there being an intermediary superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would he fall within the purview of this article if his subordinates failed to initiate a disciplinary investigation? Should he be aware of a violation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could focus next on Article 181. Again, we'll have -- in the English, we'll have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can you now explain to us Article 181 and the difference between Article 180 and 181.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic difference is that in Article 180, there is -- there are proceedings for disciplinary investigation, which is to say they're collecting elements in establishing whether there are grounds to initiate proceedings before a disciplinary court, military disciplinary court. However, an officer who orders that a disciplinary investigation be launched is not responsible or is not authorised to formally place the perpetrator under the jurisdiction of a disciplinary military court. Those powers rest with the officers who are defined in Article 182. Those officers are at a rather high position, and there weren't that many of them in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would General Perisic be one of those high-ranking officers within the meaning of Article 181?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you a variation of Article 181. This deals with the referral of a matter to a military disciplinary court. How was a matter referred to a criminal court? Is that covered by the Law on the Army, or is it outside the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, this is not provided under the provisions of this law because there was a Law on Military Courts, too, which then provided for such a procedure. It's true that officers in any kind of position did not have the authority to pass on the case to a criminal court, or perhaps they could submit the charges to the authorised military prosecutor, who would then process the case further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "process the case further"? In other words, are you suggesting, sir, that the determination whether to refer the matter to a domestic criminal court, a non-military criminal court, rests with the prosecutor for the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think perhaps it's a misunderstanding. If we're talking about the responsibility of military personnel, according to the regulations in force at that time, military personnel were criminally prosecuted before military courts, not before other types of courts, and because of that, the case would be referred to the military prosecutor who would then play the role that he has under the law to assess if there are grounds for reasonable suspicion to initiate further proceedings and to go before the investigative judge, but these are matters that I'm not actually all that knowledgeable about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Starcevic, for clarifying that point for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to Article 107. That's found at page 9 of the B/C/S and page 25 of the English. This is also a rather long article, and on the English we need to go to the second -- another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you explain the purpose and intent of this particular provision.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 107 regulates all the possible ways that a professional or a non-commissioned officer's service in the army can cease or be suspended either if it should be or has to be suspended, according to these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are these -- do these regulations -- first of all, they set forth a number of elements. We can see, for example, items 1 through 6, and then beneath item 6, we can see a reference to 30 pensionable years of service, et cetera. Are these -- is termination under one of these sub-elements mandatory, or is it discretionary? So, for example, if a person receives a negative evaluation two times in a row, does that automatically result in the termination of an officer, or is it discretionary with, for example, a superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law is formulated in such a way that in such a case it would be mandatory for service to be suspended. The officer does not have a discretionary right to assess in such a case whether his service in the army should be suspended or ceased or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So is it correct, Mr. Starcevic, to say that -- just looking at the numbered items, items 1 through 6, that if any of those elements are met, it's required that service be terminated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to the first paragraph under item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We -- I'm sorry. I just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, are we dealing with 107 or 108?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're dealing with 107, and I'm just looking for the text on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm looking for item 6 on 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We now have it. We will now have it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, let me refer you, then, to the paragraph that starts: "Military service of the professional officers ..." under item 6. If he has acquired 30 years of pensionable years of service. And then it says: "If the needs of the service so require." We see that term repeated in the next paragraph, as well, and I'd kindly ask you to tell us the meaning of that term "if the needs of the service so require."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This whole article, actually, is an expression of the specificity of the military service in general. It can be the case that for some reasons, either objective or subjective ones, in the view of the authorised officer, a person's service needs to be terminated even if he does not fulfil any of these conditions in paragraphs 1 to 6. At the same time, some of his rights also need to be protected. The person cannot be dismissed from service, let's say, after 30 years without getting the -- a pension. You cannot leave such a person without means of livelihood at a time-period in their life when it is difficult to change professions. So these reasons can be different. They can be objective reasons or subjective reasons because of circumstances of the person, but he is not someone who has received negative evaluations two times in a row or not a bad person or bad officer but simply for some reason they failed to meet some requirements. Perhaps I can give you a hypothetical reason. If you have a parachutist who weighs 130 kilograms, he can no longer be a parachutist, but there is nothing else that he is trained to do. You cannot replace him. He is occupying that post and is no longer actually able to perform those duties. So then for reasons of needs of the service, he is going to be pensioned off and given a pension that fits his years of service, and you can employ someone else in his place. Perhaps he will be awarded an apartment if he hasn't been awarded one before, but in any case, his livelihood and means of living would be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, who is it who makes that determination, what's in the needs of the service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer, according to Article 152 of the law, is authorised to decide about the termination of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I'm just looking at Article 152. I don't know if the Court would like to see that again on the monitor. Perhaps we could go back to that, since you've referred to it. I believe that is on page 38 of the English. And, Mr. Starcevic, you have a hard copy in front of you, so if you just cast your eye on Article 152 again. So, Mr. Starcevic, the first sentence reads: "The chief of the General Staff and the commanding officers of units or institutions designated by him shall ..." And then I take it that subpart (6) of this article is what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when we're talking about generals, then we need to apply the previous article, 151, paragraph (3).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. Now, in terms of defining the term we've been talking about, are there any standards or criteria that are in regulations or elsewhere, memorandum, that define the needs of the service, or is it totally subjective?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, this is a separate procedure for implementing these articles of the law. I'm not sure, though, but I think there is such a procedure, and that, in these provisions, there are examples given of needs of service, but I think ultimately that is something that is in the discretion of the officer who is making that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And does a person who is affected by a decision where he or she has been retired because of the needs of the service, have any administrative recourse or legal recourse to challenge a finding that the needs of the service require his or her termination?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is the right to appeal such a decision, and it can be submitted to the higher superior officer, and there's also a right of complaint or submitting of an appeal before the higher military administrative court. Therefore, there is -- there are legal means to appeal such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time to break. I'm going to be going into private session very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I just want to clarify a couple of points in your earlier examination. They deal with the process. How was a matter referred to criminal proceedings? How was it referred -- how -- yeah. I think that's ... was it referred to a military prosecutor? Was it referred to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the witness -- we have seen in one of the exhibits something that regulates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We saw, Your Honour -- I think what we saw was how disciplinary matters are referred, and my question is how are criminal matters referred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is always something that is processed by the prosecutor. The prosecutor, as a kind of informal act, is presented with the criminal charges. Then the prosecutor reviews that and decides whether, on the basis of evidence that he would compile, would propose the initiation of a criminal investigation. The decision on initiating an investigation is made by the court, the investigative judge conducting the investigation, returns it to the prosecutor, and decides whether the gathered evidence is sufficient to issue an indictment, and at that point, it becomes part of the court jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One question I have, Mr. Starcevic, is you say: "The Prosecutor, as a kind of an informal act, is presented with the criminal charges." Who presents the prosecutor with the criminal charges? Let me give you a hypothetical. Let's say a criminal act has been committed by a VJ soldier. How does the matter get to the prosecutor in order to prosecute the matter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in our Criminal Code, we still have - and my colleagues probably know that better - the provision that the Prosecutor is obliged to act as soon as he receives any kind of information about the commission of a criminal act in whatever way can he find out about it in the media or in any other way he can find out that there are grounds for suspicion that a criminal act was committed. But a military officer is obliged, according to military recreations, when he finds something like that out, to in turn inform the Prosecutor about it, and this is why I say it's an informal act. It's not required to be submitted in a specific form or format. Of course, it depends on the general preparedness and legal mastery of the person who actually writes this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So General Perisic would be obliged to inform the prosecutor if he found out about a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, two other brief questions. Were there functioning military disciplinary courts in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the period from 1992 through 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
