utterances.text: Yes, in 1992 they were functioning, but I didn't really follow that kind of thing anymore in the military judiciary, so I don't know what time they stopped. But, in any case, they were functioning at the time when I left the army and for a while after that, but I don't know for how long after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's Prosecution Exhibit 197.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I want to turn very briefly to Article 178. Mr. Starcevic, focussing on Article 178, it indicates that there are military disciplinary courts in the first instance established in the General Staff, the commands of the army, the air force, anti-aircraft defence, and the navy. Can you enlighten us as to what kinds of cases and -- fall within the various courts that are described in Article 178? How does it work?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we already dealt with that to an extent. But these are all cases when the officer does have grounds to assume that there is a basis for disciplinary proceedings. The way in which they are treated in the system of responsibility is that the unit officer would initiate disciplinary investigations, and then the result of that investigation, if it is evaluated that there are grounds or justified suspicion that a disciplinary violation was committed, then all the documents in the case file compiled during the investigation would be sent to that officer who is -- whose duty it is to bring the perpetrator before the military disciplinary court. The senior officer who -- or the officer who received the case file with the results of the investigation would then reach a formal decision and issue a formal written decision bringing somebody before the military disciplinary court, and that decision, together with the entire case file, would be forwarded to the prosecutor at the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't think I made myself very clear, Mr. Starcevic. What I'm talking about is, for example, if a VJ soldier who was in the navy commits a violation, is that case tried in the first instance in the military disciplinary court that's described here in Article 178, it being established in the navy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So in terms of the General Staff, then I take it subordinate units where there's a -- a disciplinary violation, that would be tried before the military disciplinary court of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And, finally, one last question: I take it all appeals from all of these previous military -- oh, forget --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour. I think it is self-evident. Let me return if I can to -- we were looking at Article 107 before the break. If I could go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 709 on the monitor, please. And I would like to, first of all, turn to B/C/S, page 24; English, page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to refresh your memory from yesterday, Mr. Starcevic, with this passage, and then we'll will explore further this session. Mr. Starcevic, this is the 14th session of the Supreme Defence Council that was held on the 11th of October, 1993, and we looked at a passage --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring the Court to the first -- the top of the page, Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm also referring you to the top of the page. There's a -- it reads: "In our orders, for instance we write them, the commander in such-and-such a unit will be deployed in a training corps which is supposed to be here, but in fact, he is going over there." Now if we could turn to B/C/S, page 25; English, page 33. And the English, I'm -- I would like to refer the Court to -- and counsel to the passage with Mr. Bulatovic at the bottom. In the English, it carries over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, now, I can't read the text, but I would like you to key in on the portion that begins: "I think it's a very sensitive question ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to page 35 of the English and page 26 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I want to direct your attention to that passage that is in the middle of the page: Momcilo Perisic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, to the passage that is at the -- under Momcilo Perisic, that first paragraph, that only paragraph. And, finally, if we could turn to the next page, page 36 in English, and page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to the passage with Mr. Bulatovic in the middle of the page, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's the only passage identified with Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, the passage that we looked at, just -- we've been looking at, there's a reference on the previous passage that -- that -- and I quote, this is General Perisic, it says: "I have already issued an internal order that they all are supposed to go there. Whoever doesn't want to go has to find a mode." It goes on to say: "If someone doesn't want to go and has over 30 years' of pensionable employment, we can give him early retirement so that we're not accepting this. We will tell him he is not performing his duties in a satisfactory manner and other things, but we won't write that he did not want to go there." It goes on to say: "We will find another way of getting rid of them." Now, can you comment on that text and the implications that that has for Article 107 of the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this way of putting questions leads to a situation where one is asking the witness to speculate. First of all, parts of a discussion that we know about have been taken out of context. One topic that is discussed on over 20 pages, a sentence is being pulled out and the witness is being asked to interpret it pursuant to the provisions of the law. And, of course, Your Honours know there is a difference between somebody commenting on text like this and having the comments of the person who participated in the actual discussion. The witness is not able to really comment here, and Mr. Harmon here is trying to get the witness to comment on matters that are not directly in his experience. So, in a way, we're getting into a collision with what Mr. Starcevic said before in terms of the time when this conference -- when this session was held. I think that there must be a difference in the comments that Mr. Starcevic is making regarding this type of document and regarding a law that you have in front of you and are able to also look at yourselves. I don't want to be -- well, perhaps it seems as if I'm complicating things. I do not wish to be suggesting anything in my objection, but we know when the law was adopted and when this Session was held, and now the witness is being asked to comment. So even though this is a factual witness, he is not able to talk about things that he personally doesn't know. I mean, he was able to comment and give some explanations of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I reframe the question then, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, the text that I recited to you dealing with a person who has over 30 years' of pensionable employment, does that implicate Article 107 of the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I would like to ask Mr. Harmon to say when these words were spoken. Again, we're talking about something, a sentence that was spoken before the law went into effect, and then we need to also specify the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stated that the 14th Session was held on the 11th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're right. And when did the law come in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness testified yesterday - I have to -- let me just ask him. He testified that the Law on the Army was initially promulgated, and then there was a year period of time during which time they had to reconcile one provision, but the law was in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, let me just ask you, when did the Law on the Army come into effect? Let me ask you again.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the copy that I have in front of me, I'm not able to really determine the exact date. Actually, it's clear to me from the copy that I have that the time when the Chamber or the council adopted the draft law, but in order to know when the law went into effect, I would need to know the date it was published in the Official Gazette because a law goes into effect on the eighth day following its publication in the Official Gazette. And I'm sorry, but I'm unable to see that from the copy that I have in front of me. I can just say when this final version of the law was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document you are holding in your hands, sir, is that not an Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is. But I have to point out that this law, in keeping with the constitutional practice of sorts, actually came into effect twice, the first time when it was adopted at the Chamber of Citizens, but the Chamber of republics did not adopt an identical text, so that it was in effect from that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After it was adopted by the Chamber of Citizens, was it published in the Gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes. But that Official Gazette --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the constitution provides that the text shall be applicable until it is finally reconciled in both Chambers, or before both Chambers, within no later than a year's time. So, in fact, it was in effect as of then, and then the newer version, the reconciled version, was published in this Official Gazette, so that as a consequence, because it was published in the Official Gazette on the 27th of May, 1994, this would mean that it came into effect on the 5th or 6th of June, 1994. But this relates to this version, the reconciled version. As for when the first version came into effect, I would need to see that Official Gazette where that version was actually published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does this mean, then, we can only go by the date of the document you have in your hands, which is dated the 27th of May, 1994? That's the document we have before Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be able to assist the Chamber on this because yesterday when I asked Mr. Starcevic this question, he gave an answer. It's found at page 5437 at line 7, and I can read the answer, if you care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at 5436, line 14, I asked

utterances.speaker: MR. STARCEVIC
utterances.text: "When did the Law on the Army become effective? What date?" And then, thereupon, Mr. Starcevic explained that the problem that he has explained again today, that there was a difficulty between the two texts and they had to be reconciled. He then answered at 5437, starting at line 5, he said: "So in other words, this law came into effect in the form that it was adopted in the Chamber of Citizens at the end of May, I believe -- no, I apologise, in October 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I'm aware of that. I thought the concern, that we have him here in court, he has got a document in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's dated 27th of May, 1994. It takes effect on the 6th of June, 1994, according to what he tells us, and that is the -- seems to me to be that the version that has been ratified by both Chambers of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what the witness answered, as I understood his evidence - I'm trying to find it precisely - but I understood his evidence was when there is a discrepancy in the text, the law goes into effect. There is a one-year period during which time there is efforts between the two Chambers, the two Houses to reconcile that language, and thereafter, the -- that happened within the one-year period of time, and thereafter, the text was officially adopted. But it had been in effect, according to Mr. Starcevic's answer, since October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if an issue arises within the year that requires the unresolved provision to be applied, what then happens?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to defer to Mr. Starcevic on that one provision. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the version that was adopted in the Chamber of Citizens is applicable until the final reconciliation of versions, and, of course, I'm not denying that this text actually took effect in October, but I just don't know the exact date in October, and if I understood this whole discussion well, what is contested here, or, rather, what is a matter of contest between the two parties is the date and not the month. And when looking at this text, it would seem to me that that could not have been before the 20th of October, but I'm not certain and can't be until I see the actual version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is on his feet. Let's give him -- yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have before me a page of the military gazette. Perhaps we can put it on the ELMO, and perhaps the witness can read from it. This is an official military gazette which speaks of when this Law on the Army of Yugoslavia was adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly asks that the counsel repeat the date when this was published in the military gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The counsel didn't mention the date because that's precisely what he wants us to see on the ELMO, and he doesn't want to testify. I'm answering the interpreter. You want to show it to your colleagues before you put it on the ELMO, if you so wish?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that would be proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't read it. Unfortunately, I can't read it. It's very kind of you, Mr. Novak [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If you can't read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is in Cyrillic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't approve it. You can't approve that it goes on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't have an interpreter here, Your Honour, and I can't. But I'm willing to accept what -- perhaps Mr. Lukic can read the text into the record, and I would be satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would probably be best if the witness were to read this portion of the text and also to interpret what date this would be and when it was published. Of course, I can read, but I think it would be the most objective approach if the witness were to read this, just the portion that relates to when this provisional text was actually published in the military Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold on, Mr. ... Mr. Harmon must still grant his permission before anything is shown to the witness. That's why it went to him in the first place, and he suggested that you read it, and he will accept what you say. So if you still say it must go to the witness, Mr. Harmon must still say: Even though I'm illiterate in this language, I still agree that it be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm satisfied that Mr. Starcevic can read it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can give it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The law was published on the 4th of November, 1993, in the Official Gazette, number 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, then let me just explore this a bit further with you. Prior to the promulgation of the Law on the Army, was there a law that was replaced, and what was the name of that law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a law, the name of which was the Law on Service in the Armed Forces; and in fact, it was superceded by this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Law on Service in the Armed Forces have a provision that related to the reasons for termination of professional military service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that previous law have an article that was similar to Article 107 in the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a similar article.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the law on the -- the previous law have a provision that dealt with the termination from professional military service of a professional officer who had acquired at least 30 years' of pensionable service, if the needs of the service so required?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there was such a provision, but also some other provisions. In other words, this article, 107, is not identical to the one that existed in the earlier law, but I think there was a provision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, we have an exhibit, or 65 ter number. We have the Law on Service in the Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With counsel's permission, and since I didn't notify counsel of the -- that I would be using this with Mr. Starcevic, we can resolve the issue very quickly if I could call up the Law on the Service of Armed Forces. It is it 65 ter 5839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a problem with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, and I know you absolutely prepared for e-court and not otherwise, but do you have any extra copies of these laws that we have been working on this morning? I mean, we're going backwards and forwards through many of these articles, at times without having to put the article back on the monitor. Maybe it might help if we just have it and can flip through -- if you don't have, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I may, Your Honour. Your Honour, we have one set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We can share.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can put on the monitor the old law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 5839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, 5830.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Starcevic, while the old law comes up on the monitor, do you by chance -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be feasible for the needs of the transcript to show this document that we placed on the ELMO to actually admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mean the -- the earlier document that Mr. Lukic showed to the parties, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I have no objection to it being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we give it a 65 ter number, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we don't have a 65 ter number for that document because we just pulled it out in hard copy right now. Perhaps we can forward it to the registrar later on. I don't know what the easiest way to do this would be. Perhaps we can just assign the next number in the 65 ter series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay. Okay, Mr. Lukic. Okay, the registrar has a way you can tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She knows how to work it out. Just tender it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I move to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D81, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a proposal. I think rather than trying to search through the monitor and trying to find the exact provision that I -- Mr. Starcevic referred to, the parallel provision in the previous law, I have a hard copy in the Serbian language. If I could present that to Mr. Starcevic after showing it to counsel, then he can find it for us a lot faster than we can do on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If this could first be shown to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, it may be Article 392.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Article 392.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify the passage that may be similar to the article in the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we mean the hard copy pages, that would be on page 290, following item -- or Article 4. There is an paragraph that makes a reference to the special needs of the service and the interests of the armed forces, and only upon a decision by the Presidency of the SFRY and in such a -- such an event, a professional soldier did not enjoy the guaranteed rights that were actually recognised in the provision in the new law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a bit lost. I'm not quite sure where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was looking at an English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, what I'm trying to find and if you can direct us to a provision that is similar in the old law that relates to termination from service for a person who has served at least 30 pensionable years of service if the needs of the service so require. Is there such a provision in the old law that is before -- that is in your hand?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I tried to do. Under the old law, the criterion was not the years of service but the special needs of the service and interests of the armed forces, regardless of the years of service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might ask you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about -- if you look at Article 392, you have Roman numerals I to VI, and then the next paragraph of Roman numerals I to V, and then the next one says: The service of an active duty service men may terminate, column 1, when he completes 40 (men) or 35 (women) years of pensionable service if the needs of the service so require. Isn't that it? Just the difference of time of service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This provision, in effect, provides for the regular retirement of professional soldiers because the condition for retirement under the system which existed in the armed forces was 40 years of service for men and 35 years of service for women, and this was one of the regular ways for termination of service for an individual who has met the requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. But Mr. Harmon's question had been, and at page 66, line 14: "Mr. Starcevic, what I'm trying to find and if can you direct to us to a provision that is similar in the old law that relates to termination from service for a person who has served at least 30 pensionable years if the needs of service so require." Isn't that also just a regular termination after a specified number of years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such a provision did not exist in the old law, but the similarities between the old and the new law were in the reasons provided for termination of service when required by the needs of the service, and such a provision as the needs require did exist in the old law following number 4, after number 4. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which number 4? There are many number 4s here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first paragraph, we have numbers 1 to 6. In the second paragraph, we have 1 to 5. And then we have numbers from 1 to 4. Following that number 4, the reason for termination of service that is given is the needs of the service. However, at that time, this did not -- was not limited by that criterion of 30 years of service, so that any individual could be terminated because of the needs of the service, regardless of the number of years that they had spent in the army, the number of years of service, and that is where it differs from the new law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't see the entire text of the law in the English version on the screen, so yeah, we accept -- I'll accept what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That is what I had earlier described as the specific aspect of military service, the reflection of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. But I don't -- I don't know whether you are saying this is the counterpart of the new law. I think the counterpart that Mr. Harmon was looking for is what I'd referred you to. I don't know. What do you say, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, there is the new text in Article 107 in the Law on the Army, and as I understand your evidence, there are similarities but not mirror images of the new law in the older version of the article have you read us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So the principle of the needs of the service, one of the factors that was considered under the old law was how many years you had been in the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific aspect of the service is based on the criterion that there should be the needs and interests of the service. They should be in existence, and that was the basic criterion in both of these texts we are discussing. When we were drafting the new proposal, we as lawyers considered it unfair as well as legally untenable that a man may be terminated based on the needs of the service, a man at the end of his career, without protecting that man's rights, and that is why this article was amended in the sense that the new text provides that this is possible only if that worker or that serviceman has already had 30 years of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, did the concept of the needs of the service change between the old law and the new law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think that it changed much. It still remained as the criterion for the termination of service. But it changed to the extent that the basic rights of the personnel were preserved in the event that there were such needs of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can we go back to the exhibit, the previous exhibit, which is 709, and I would like to go to B/C/S, page 26, and English, page 35, and re-visit that particular text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, under the Law of the Army, if an active military officer received an order to go to a particular duty post and he refused, would that be a -- what consequences would flow from that refusal under the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, he would have to carry out the order and then appeal against it, but the appeal itself would not postpone the execution of the order. If he would definitely refuse, then that could serve as a grounds for disciplinary responsibility of the person, and if I remember correctly, in some cases there would be also criminal charges involved, because according to the criminal law at the time, among the violations of military discipline would be a refusal to execute an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you to examine the text that's before you, where General Perisic is -- it's on the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it has been highlighted for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says: "I have already issued an internal order that they're all supposed to go there; whoever doesn't go has to find a mode; we, too, have found the appropriate criteria." And then it goes on to say: "If someone doesn't want to go and has over 30 years experience [sic], years of pensionable employment ..." We will give him early retirement, essentially, and they discuss -- it goes on: "We'll tell him that is he not performing his duties in a satisfactory manner ... but we won't write that he did not want to go there." Now, not wanting to go to a duty assignment was an actionable offence under the VJ. You've just said that, correct, under the law on the VJ. Not accepting an assignment had consequences.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when a -- when an officer refuses to accept an assignment, is it the practice in the Yugoslav Army to find a -- another basis by which to terminate a -- an officer, as opposed to utilising the refusal to go and accept an order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that if we're talking about a fact witness and things that are known to the witness as facts, but Mr. Harmon is now asking the witness about things that he generally knows, so then he is being asked to provide an expert opinion. Perhaps the witness can be asked if he specifically knows and has some experience about that but not to be asked for a general assessment about some matters because then that would mean that he would be giving an expert witness reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the witness the question on the basis that he has a long-standing and serving -- he was a career military officer. That's the basis for the question, and I think he can give an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether this question is calling for an opinion, or is it calling for knowledge on the part of the witness whether there was any legal provision in the laws that he drafted that covers the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not ask him that -- the question with that intention. I asked him the question on the -- on the basis that he had 30 -- or many years in military service and in his experience, and perhaps I need to frame it that way, but in his experience, has he seen a situation where there are efforts to conceal the basis of the termination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think I will overrule the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember encountering such cases during my work. I don't think that I encountered anything like that in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, could I tender the document, the Law on The service of the Armed Forces as an exhibit that was referred to and we discussed for a number of minutes. It's 65 ter number 5830. And if -- Your Honour, it's a long document. We're satisfied to have the article that was referred to at this point in time be the Prosecution Exhibit and not the whole exhibit, unless counsel has a desire to do it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would rather have the entire law admitted because the law was in effect formally until March 1994, and it's important for this case, so if I am being asked, then I would propose that the whole law be tendered for admission. I'm also probably going to be asking the witness questions on it during my cross-examination later. And the problem is that the version in e-court actually is not the translation of the complete law, so perhaps we can then at least have the whole law in the B/C/S loaded onto the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you want it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the entire text is not translated into English. I have been informed that only ten pages of it have been translated, so marked for identification until the entire law is translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That imposes -- I think there was a reason why the entire law wasn't translated into English, because it's a massive text. If the admission now of the whole document requires the translation of the whole text, then I would be perfectly satisfied to keep the portions of the text that are translated admitted, and then I will go back and examine the feasibility of translating the remaining portions of the text. I think a large number of the portion of the text is irrelevant, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think the Chamber is going to admit the pages that you have used today, and if the Defence uses other pages later, the pages that they use will be admitted. So pages -- the relevant pages of Exhibit 5830 or 65 ter 5830 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those pages would be Exhibit P2305.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to embark on a rather lengthy topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you embark on the lengthy topic, Judge Picard would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you still need the documents that are on the screen? Oh, you do. Can we stay in private session. Don't answer, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Starcevic, I am asking a question that has to do with these two laws, the old and the new laws on the army. It seems at the point in time when this meeting was held, the text that is in front of us -- actually, at the time of the meeting the new law had not yet gone into effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it seems to be like that. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I don't understand anymore why at this meeting Mr. Perisic quite clearly referred to Article 107 that still was not in effect because nowhere in the old law was the possibility mentioned of termination of service in the army after 30 years' of pensionable service. This is not quite clear to me why General Perisic, in this part here, refers to these 30 years. Does that have anything to do with some kind of provision that was in the old law, or is this new law -- was it already existing, was it already drafted, and was it possible that he is referring here to some future new law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that everything that you said is really quite possible. I don't know why he refers to it, but it is a fact that at that time the law was completed, and it was already being discussed in the parliament. It's a fact that in the preparation of the law, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia also took part, so that was an expected resolution or a manner to deal with that particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in order to have everything quite clear, when you refer to 30 years of service, or 30 years of pensionable service - I'm not quite sure what the term is - is that something that was also in the old law? We saw that it was 40 years for men and 35 years for women. Was that something that was part of the old law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the old Law on The Armed Services, this was not there. I could maybe make a comparison, but this is already compared between termination of service and one's right to pension. A special law laid down the conditions under which one secures the right to a pension, and in that law, this right to pension, depended on the years of service and -- and age, as well, so I can just give you an example. For example, a man who is 65 years old can have over 20 years of service and have the right to a pension. Perhaps this is some kind of link there, but I'm not really able to tell you definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when we're talking about 30 years of pensionable service, there is no basis for that in the old law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, judge. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, noting the time, I have no additional questions. Can we go back into public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the Chamber please move into open session, and may we remove the exhibits from the screen before we go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes. You say you have got no questions for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No questions for the day, Your Honour. I'd ask that Mr. Starcevic return, and I need to resolve with Mr. Starcevic a set of dates with him when he can return. We had discussed it earlier, but now I'm not able to talk to him, and I have been informed of an element that has changed my previous planning by one day, and I need to be able to talk through an intermediary or have an intermediary discuss with Mr. Starcevic a convenient date when he can return. May I make -- what I had initially planned and suggested to counsel and to Mr. Starcevic was that he return on the 11th and 12th of May, but I was informed just before this session began that -- through the court officer that Mr. Starcevic is unable to fly on the 10th, which would eliminate the possibility of his testifying on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I would -- I know my schedule, but I need to talk some details with -- through an intermediary with Mr. Starcevic so I can finally resolve the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that after the break you talk with Mr. Starcevic in the presence of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is satisfactory, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And sort out the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. But the court can still adjourn to a specific date on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Starcevic, it does look like we're not able to finish with your testimony. You'll have to come back someday. You will have to talk to counsel and other counsel and sort out whatever is convenient for you, and they will let us know when you come. Other than that discussion for the postponement of the date, as you know, are you not supposed to talk to anybody, in particular with your counsel, until you are excused from testifying. We'll see you when you next come. The Court stands adjourned until Monday, the 27th of April, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of April, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
